Section 1.1 of Lock⁵ introduces the anatomy of a dataset: **cases** are the units
we observe (one row per case), and **variables** are characteristics recorded on
every case (one column per variable). A variable is **quantitative** when its
values are numbers for which arithmetic makes sense (heights, salaries, counts)
and **categorical** when it places each case into a group (yes/no answers,
brands, regions). When one variable helps explain or predict another, the first
is the **explanatory variable** and the second is the **response variable**.
The exercises below are from *Statistics: Unlocking the Power of Data*
(Lock⁵, 3rd ed., pp. 13–17). Skill Builders 1.1–1.10 drill the definitions; the
rest apply them to real studies, and tabs based on Lock5 data files include a
small executable EDA.


## Exercise 1.1

**People in a city are asked if they support a new recycling law.**
*(Skill Builder 1: (a) the cases, (b) the variable and its type.)*

- **(a) Cases:** the people in the city who were asked (the residents surveyed).
- **(b) Variable:** whether the person supports the new recycling law
  (support / do not support) — **categorical**, since it records group
  membership rather than a number on which arithmetic makes sense.

## Exercise 1.2

**Record the percentage change in the price of a stock for 100 stocks publicly
traded on Wall Street.**

- **(a) Cases:** the 100 stocks.
- **(b) Variable:** percentage change in the stock's price — **quantitative**,
  a numerical value where differences and averages are meaningful.

- **(b) Variable:** whether the country's literacy rate is over 75% (yes / no) —

## Exercise 1.11

**Student Survey Variables (Data 1.1).** Example 1.2 already classified seven
of the variables in `StudentSurvey`; the remaining variables are `Year`,
`Height`, `Weight`, `Siblings`, `VerbalSAT`, `MathSAT`, `SAT`, and
`HigherSAT`.

**(a) Quantitative or categorical?**

| Variable | Description | Type |
|---|---|---|
| Year | FirstYear / Sophomore / Junior / Senior | categorical |
| Height | height in inches | quantitative |
| Weight | weight in pounds | quantitative |
| Siblings | number of siblings | quantitative |
| VerbalSAT | Verbal SAT score | quantitative |
| MathSAT | Math SAT score | quantitative |
| SAT | Verbal + Math SAT combined | quantitative |
| HigherSAT | which SAT section is higher | categorical |

**(b) Questions about an individual variable**, e.g. “What is the average
height of students in the survey?” or “How many students are seniors?” — any

**(c) Questions about relationships**, e.g. “Do taller students tend to weigh
more?” or “Do students with a higher VerbalSAT score also tend to have a
higher MathSAT score?”

*Data:* `data/ch01/StudentSurvey.csv` (Data 1.1, n = 362), downloaded from

## Exercise 1.13

**Goldilocks Effect: Read to Your Kids!** 27 four-year-olds heard stories in
three formats (audio, illustrated, animated) while an MRI machine measured
each child's brain connectivity. Illustrated was “just right.”

- **(a) Explanatory variable:** story format (audio / illustrated / animated) —

## Exercise 1.14

**Female Gamers Face Sexual Harassment.** A research firm questioned 1151
female gamers in Great Britain.

- **(a) Cases:** the 1151 female gamers who were questioned.
- **(b) Variables:** whether the gamer had received obscene messages while

## Exercise 1.15

**Active Learning vs Passive Learning: Which is Best?** Students in a college
physics course were randomly assigned to an active-learning or a
passive-learning class period; afterwards they rated how much they thought
they had learned (1–5 Likert scale) and took a 20-question multiple-choice exam.

- **(a) Cases:** the students who took part in the study.
- **(b) Variables:** teaching format, active vs passive (**categorical**);
  perceived learning, the 1–5 Likert rating (**quantitative**, though ordinal);
  actual learning, the score on the 20-question exam (**quantitative**).
- **(c) Explanatory variable:** teaching format. **Response variables:**
  perceived learning and exam score (two responses measured on each student).
- **(d) Dataset size:** 154 + 142 = **296 rows** and **3 columns**.

The interesting finding: students *thought* they learned more passively but
*actually* learned more in the active class — a gap between perceived and real
learning.

## Exercise 1.16

**Spider Sex Play.** Some maturing spiders were allowed to take part in
near-matings (mock sex); others were isolated. When fully mature, pairs with
mock-sex experience reached real mating significantly faster.

- **Cases:** the pairs of spiders observed at real matings.
- **Variables:** whether either partner had prior near-mating experience
  (yes / no) — **categorical**, the explanatory variable; time to reach real
  mating — **quantitative**, the response variable.

## Exercise 1.17

**Hormones and Fish Fertility.** Water samples were taken from various lakes;
as estrogen concentration rises, fish fertility falls.

- **Cases:** the lakes (the water samples taken from lakes).
- **Variables:** estrogen concentration in the lake water, in parts per
  trillion — **quantitative**, the explanatory variable; fertility of the fish,
  recorded as the percent of eggs fertilized — **quantitative**, the response
  variable.

## Exercise 1.18

**Fast-Twitch Muscles and Race.** A study of the *ACTN3* gene variant reported
it in about 20% of a sample of Caucasians, 25% of a sample of Asians, and 1%
of a sample of Africans.

- **Cases:** the people in the three samples.
- **Variables:** ethnic group (Caucasian / Asian / African) — **categorical**;

## Exercise 1.19

**Largest Cities in the World.** Seven of the ten largest cities (including
the largest, Tokyo, Japan) are in the Eastern Hemisphere and three are in the
Western Hemisphere. Table 1.3 gives populations in millions:
Eastern — 37, 26, 23, 22, 21, 21, 21; Western — 21, 20, 19.

- **(a)** There are **10 cases** (the ten largest cities) and **two
  variables**: Hemisphere (Eastern / Western) — **categorical** — and
  Population, in millions — **quantitative**.
- **(b)** The dataset with cases as rows and variables as columns:

*The printed table gives only populations grouped by hemisphere (city names
are not recorded), so rows are identified by rank.*

```{python}
#| echo: false
cities = pd.DataFrame({
    "Hemisphere": ["Eastern"] * 7 + ["Western"] * 3,
    "Population": [37, 26, 23, 22, 21, 21, 21, 21, 20, 19],
})
cities
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Populations of the ten largest cities, colored by hemisphere"
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.2))
for hemi, color in [("Eastern", "#4c72b0"), ("Western", "#c44e52")]:
    sub = cities[cities["Hemisphere"] == hemi]
    ax.bar(sub.index + 1, sub["Population"], color=color, label=hemi)
ax.set_xlabel("City (ranked by population)")
ax.set_ylabel("Population (millions)")
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Exercise 1.20

**How Fast Do Homing Pigeons Go?** In the 2019 Midwest Classic (Topeka,
Kansas) the fastest bird went 1676 YPM (yards per minute), about 56 mph. The
top seven finishers included three Hens (females) and four Cocks (males).
Table 1.4 gives speeds in YPM: Hens — 1676, 1452, 1449; Cocks — 1458, 1435,
1418, 1413.

- **(a)** There are **7 cases** (the top seven finishers) and **two
  variables**: Sex (Hen / Cock) — **categorical** — and Speed, in YPM —
  **quantitative**.
- **(b)** The dataset with cases as rows and variables as columns:

```{python}
#| echo: false
pigeons = pd.DataFrame({
    "Sex": ["Hen"] * 3 + ["Cock"] * 4,
    "Speed": [1676, 1452, 1449, 1458, 1435, 1418, 1413],
})
pigeons
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Race speeds of the top seven homing pigeons, by sex"
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.5, 3))
for sex, color in [("Hen", "#c44e52"), ("Cock", "#4c72b0")]:
    sub = pigeons[pigeons["Sex"] == sex]
    ax.scatter(sub["Sex"], sub["Speed"], s=70, color=color, label=sex)
ax.set_ylabel("Speed (YPM)")
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Exercise 1.21

**Pigeon Racing.** In the 2019 Midwest Classic, 1412 pigeons finished the
race, and each bird's home loft, sex, distance, and speed were recorded.

- **(a) Cases:** 1412 (the pigeons that finished the race).
- **(b) Variables:** 4 in total — home loft (**categorical**), sex
  (**categorical**), distance (**quantitative**), speed (**quantitative**).
  So 2 categorical and 2 quantitative.
- **(c) Dataset size:** 1412 rows and 4 columns. A loft may have several

## Exercise 1.22

**Trans-Generational Effects of Diet.** Male rats were fed a high-fat diet or
a normal diet; their daughters (who never ate a high-fat diet) were far more
likely to develop metabolic syndrome if the father ate high-fat food.

- **Variables:** the father's diet (high-fat vs normal) — **categorical**,
  the explanatory variable; whether the daughter develops metabolic syndrome
  (yes / no) — **categorical**, the response variable.

Both main variables are categorical.

## Exercise 1.23

**Trans-Generational Effects of Environment.** Young female mice were assigned
to an enriched environment or not; their adult offspring learned to navigate
mazes faster even though they had never been exposed to the enrichment.

- **Variables:** the mother's environment (enriched vs not enriched) —
  **categorical**, the explanatory variable; intelligence of the offspring,
  measured by how fast they learn to navigate mazes — **quantitative**, the
  response variable (it could be reduced to a smarter / not-smarter label, but
  as measured it is quantitative).

## Exercise 1.24

**Pennsylvania High School Seniors.** The data in `PASeniors` show results for
a sample of 457 high-school seniors in Pennsylvania, selected at random from
students in the Census at Schools project between 2010 and 2019. For each
question, decide whether the answer gives a value for a **quantitative
variable**, a **categorical variable**, or is **not a value for a variable**
in this dataset.

- **(a)** What mode of transportation do you use to get to school?
  → **Categorical** — the answer (Car / Bus / Walk) is a value of the variable
  `GetToSchool`.
- **(b)** Do you have any allergies? → **Categorical** (Yes / No), the variable
  `Allergies`.
- **(c)** What proportion of students in this sample are vegetarians?
  → **Not a value for a variable**: it is a summary statistic computed across
  all 457 cases. The case-level variable `Vegetarian` (Yes / No) is
  categorical.
- **(d)** How many hours did you spend last week working at a paid job?
  → **Quantitative**, the variable `WorkHours`.
- **(e)** What is the difference between typical hours of sleep you get on
  school nights and non-school nights? → **Not a value for a variable in this
  dataset** as recorded: the file stores two separate quantitative variables
  (`Sleep1`, `Sleep2`), and their per-student difference, while quantitative
  in nature, is a derived quantity rather than one of the recorded variables.
- **(f)** What is the maximum time (in minutes) that a student in this sample
  needs to get to school? → **Not a value for a variable**: the maximum is a
  summary statistic over all cases. The case-level variable `TravelTime` is
  quantitative.
- **(g)** If you could have a super power — invisibility, telepathy, super
  strength, ability to fly, or ability to freeze time? → **Categorical**, the
  variable `Superpower`.

*Data:* `data/ch01/PASeniors.csv` (n = 457, 36 variables), downloaded from
<https://www.lock5stat.com/datasets3e/PASeniors.csv>.

```{python}
#| echo: false
pas = pd.read_csv("data/ch01/PASeniors.csv")
pas[["GetToSchool", "Allergies", "Vegetarian", "WorkHours",
     "Sleep1", "Sleep2", "TravelTime", "Superpower"]].head()
```

The summary quantities in (c) and (f) live at the sample level, not the case
level:

```{python}
#| echo: false
pd.DataFrame({
    "Summary quantity": ["Proportion vegetarian", "Max travel time (min)"],
    "Value": [(pas["Vegetarian"] == "Yes").mean().round(3),
              pas["TravelTime"].max()],
})
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "How the 457 Pennsylvania seniors get to school"
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3))
pas["GetToSchool"].value_counts().plot.bar(ax=ax, color="#4c72b0")
ax.set_xlabel("GetToSchool")
ax.set_ylabel("Students")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Exercise 1.25

**US College Scorecard.** The data in `CollegeScores` contain information from
the US Department of Education's College Scorecard on all postsecondary
educational institutions in the US. For each question, decide whether the
answer gives a value for a **quantitative variable**, a **categorical
variable**, or is **not a value for a variable** in this dataset.

- **(a)** What is the total tuition and fees for in-state students at the
  school? → **Quantitative** — a dollar amount, the variable `TuitionIn`.
- **(b)** How many of these schools are located in the Northeast? → **Not a
  value for a variable**: it is a count computed across all cases. The
  case-level variable `Region` (Northeast / Midwest / Southeast / West /
  Territory) is categorical.
- **(c)** Is the school public, private, or for profit? → **Categorical**, the
  variable `Control` (Public / Private / Profit).
- **(d)** How many undergraduates are enrolled at the school? →
  **Quantitative**, the variable `Enrollment`.
- **(e)** What percentage of undergraduates at the school are part-time
  students? → **Quantitative**, the variable `PartTime`.
- **(f)** Which school has the highest average faculty salary? → **Not a value
  for a variable**: the answer names a case (a school) singled out by a summary
  statistic. The case-level variable `FacSalary` (average faculty salary) is
  quantitative.

*Data:* `data/ch01/CollegeScores.csv` (n = 6141, 37 variables), downloaded
from <https://www.lock5stat.com/datasets3e/CollegeScores.csv>.

```{python}
#| echo: false
cs = pd.read_csv("data/ch01/CollegeScores.csv")
cs[["Name", "Control", "Region", "Enrollment", "PartTime",
    "TuitionIn", "FacSalary"]].head()
```

Like (c) and (f) in Exercise 1.24, the quantities in (b) and (f) live at the
sample level, not the case level:

```{python}
#| echo: false
pd.DataFrame({
    "Sample-level quantity": ["Schools in the Northeast",
                              "School with the highest faculty salary"],
    "Value": [(cs["Region"] == "Northeast").sum(),
              cs.loc[cs["FacSalary"].idxmax(), "Name"]],
})
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Public, private, and for-profit institutions in the College Scorecard data"
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3))
cs["Control"].value_counts().plot.bar(ax=ax, color="#4c72b0")
ax.set_xlabel("Control")
ax.set_ylabel("Schools")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Exercise 1.26

**Hookahs and Health.** Hookahs are waterpipes used for smoking flavored
tobacco. One study of 3770 university students in North Carolina found that
40% had smoked a hookah at least once, many claiming the smoke is safer than
cigarette smoke. A second study observed people at a hookah bar; a third
measured tar, nicotine, and heavy metals in samples of hookah smoke. For each
of the three studies, identify the individual cases, the variables, and
whether each variable is quantitative or categorical.

- **Study 1 (the survey):** cases are the 3770 university students; variables:
  whether the student has ever smoked a hookah (yes / no) — **categorical**;
  beliefs about the safety of hookah smoke vs cigarette smoke —
  **categorical**.
- **Study 2 (the hookah bar):** cases are the people (smoking sessions)
  observed; variables: length of the session — **quantitative**; frequency of
  puffing — **quantitative**; depth of inhalation — **quantitative**.
- **Study 3 (the chemical analysis):** cases are the samples of hookah smoke;
  variables: the amount of tar, nicotine, and heavy metals in the sample —
  each **quantitative**.

## Exercise 1.27

**Is Your Nose Getting Bigger?** Unlike most body parts, noses and ears keep
growing throughout our lifetime. A study recorded the sex of its 859
participants and reported "Age significantly influenced all analyzed

- **(a)** Six variables are mentioned: age, sex, and the four nasal

## Exercise 1.28

**Don't Text While Studying!** For the 2015 Intel Science Fair, two brothers
recruited 47 classmates: each read two passages and answered questions on
both, with no distractions for one passage and incoming text messages while
reading the other. Scores were significantly worse when texting — even for
students confident of their multitasking abilities.

- **(a) Cases:** the 47 classmates who took part in the study.
- **(b) Variables:** score on the passage read without distractions —
  **quantitative**; score on the passage read while receiving texts —
  **quantitative**; whether the participant thinks they are good at
  multitasking (yes / no) — **categorical**.
- **(c) Dataset size:** 47 rows and 3 columns.

## Exercise 1.29

**Help for Insomniacs.** Forty people diagnosed with insomnia were randomly
divided into two groups of 20 each; one group received a one-hour cognitive
behavioral therapy (CBT) session, the other received no treatment. Three
months later, 14 of the therapy group reported sleep improvements vs only 3 in
the other group.

- **(a) Cases:** the 40 people diagnosed with insomnia in the study.
- **(b) Variables:** treatment received (CBT session vs no treatment) —
  **categorical**; whether sleep improved three months later (yes / no) —
  **categorical**.
- **(c) Dataset size:** 40 rows and 2 columns.

## Exercise 1.30

**How Are Age and Income Related?** An economist collects data from many
people; how the information is recorded determines whether the variables are
quantitative or categorical.

- **Both quantitative:** record each person's age in years and income in
  dollars, so each variable takes numerical values for which arithmetic
  (differences, averages) makes sense.
- **Both categorical:** record each person's age as an age group (e.g., under
  30 / 30–50 / over 50) and income as an income bracket (e.g., under \$30k /
  \$30k–\$60k / over \$60k), so each variable simply places people into
  groups.
